name: The Battalion of Six
title: The Feyward Session Where Hjumpik Was Handed Six People at Breakfast, Named Five of Them Wrong, Lost Two Before the Roll Call, Ordered Nobody to Shoot Anybody on Purpose, Watched Waluigi Water a Tree, Held a Corridor with a Waiter and a Goblin, Read the Revel Its Own Evacuation Order Back to It, and Ended the Night Arguing About Which Living Creature Should Run at a Monster First
date: 1 Aethel, 922 BF (Feyward clock) — from the morning after the map until the wood came through the wall; the Material stood in 1040 BF, and the cutting lane outside was having its own night on the same clock, which is why nobody in the manor could say what hour it was
era: Raventree Crisis — Feyward Operations / The Battalion of Six
location: The Overgrown Manor — the heir's war room and map table, the outside wall walk, the lower service hall, the kitchen, the mushroom coat room door, and the corridor the wood came through
type: Feyward Small-Unit Command / Casualty Management / Four Engagements / Bait Planning
status: Unresolved — four engagements fought, the wood pushed back one corridor, the bait plan agreed and not yet executed; the Revel has not ended and has issued an evacuation order for its own house
summary: The morning after the map, the heir of the manor handed Hjumpik six people and a pincer. Two of the six were already dead, one of them a waiter, and the dwarf spent the rest of the day trying to keep the other four alive with an order that lasted four minutes: no friendly fire, please. Waluigi was made second-in-command, disputed the wording, and put an ice lance the length of a hallway into a tree that drank it. The wood came through the wall anyway. The Revel evacuated its own house on its own authority and everybody obeyed. The session ends in the war room with a plan, a bait, and the name of a dead dwarf nobody in the archive had ever heard of: Piktor Deldkur the Third.
description:
# SIX NAMES, ONE HAMMER, AND A FAIRY WITH A BRUISED WING
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General, Second-in-Command (Disputed), from a chair he was ordered to sit in

> **Filing note.** This session continues directly from [the night of the OC ring](feyward_chop_bros_soul_ring_and_the_guard_with_no_name), which ended with the whole party standing around the heir's tactical map. It begins at that map, the next morning, and ends with a plan. Outside the walls, on the same unreliable clock, the cutting expedition was having its own night — filed separately as [Woodfellow vs. the Treant](feyward_woodfellow_vs_the_treant). The two records overlap. Neither clock agrees with the other, and the Feyward has never once apologised for it.

Waluigi was in the war room for the first hour and in a bathroom for the second, and he intends to address the bathroom before somebody else does. It was a legitimate absence. It was tactically defensible. It had running water.

What follows is a session about command. Not about who deserved it — nobody in that house deserved anything — but about what happens when a dwarf is handed six people at breakfast and told to spend them well. He spent them. Two were already dead before the roll call. One was a waiter. One of the living six put a longsword through one of the others by accident, twice, in front of everyone, and the dwarf's entire response was to ask for more brain cells.

The record of who gave the order survives: [[prop:prop_feyward_sixth_detachment_commission|a commission written in a hurry on the back of a barrel tally]], signed by nobody, listing six names and one struck through.

The wood came through the wall at some point in the middle of all this. That is filed too, because it happened, but it is not what the session was about. The session was about the argument at the end of it, in a room with a table, over which living creature should run at a monster first.

sections.name: Who Needs the Most Directive
sections.subtitle: the war room, morning, and the morale problem nobody wanted to name
sections.overview:
The map took the whole table and the morning took the whole window. Grey Feyward light came in low across the pins, and dust from the mortar they had all climbed the night before was still settling on the sixth division's ink.

The heir stood at the head of it with both hands flat on the wood, and the party stood around him in the specific arrangement of people who have been awake too long: Hjumpik square-on, arms folded; Toad Lee leaning on his axe with his chin on his fist; Waluigi seated, because Waluigi had claimed the only chair before anyone thought to check whether the chair was claimed.

“The question,” Hjumpik said, “is who needs the most directive.”

Somebody at the door said the house was half drunk and half lazy, and that the drunk half was at least standing up. A guard with a towel over his elbow agreed. Another said the barrels were gone, all of them, splintered under a tree, and that the house had gone dry in a single night the way a pond goes dry in a summer.

“So we get more,” said the first guard.

“More drink.”

“For morale.”

“It grows,” Hjumpik said. He did not raise his voice. He said it the way a man reads a number off a page. “You feed it, it grows. Then the Revel is bigger and we are still this tired. That is the whole arithmetic.”

The room went quiet in the way rooms do when the arithmetic is correct and nobody likes it. Someone said, quietly, *not the Revel*. Hjumpik turned the idea over out loud: not the Revel — the Revelmaster. Go for the one holding the music.

“Then they turn on us,” said the guard with the towel. “Every soul in this house. You take the music away from a Revel and you are not a liberator, you are the man who stopped the party.”

“They won't turn on us if we're helping them,” Hjumpik said. “We take the plant out of their house. That is help. That is a favour with teeth in it.”

“And after?”

“After,” said the dwarf, “we worry about after.”

*WAH. I sat through that whole table. I have sat through four hundred negotiations and this is the first one conducted entirely in the future tense. Feed it, it grows. Take the music, they riot. Help them, they might not notice. Every answer in that room was a bill with the amount left blank, and every man at that table signed anyway. I did not stop them.*
sections.waluigi_note: The war room reached its operating principle before it reached its plan: act now, price it later. That is not stupidity. It is what a house does when the alternative to acting is listening to the music for one more day.

sections.name: The Dwarf Way
sections.subtitle: top to bottom, not all at once
sections.overview:
Hjumpik pointed at the prince with his chin. “He has some say, right. Mr. Prince.”

The heir of the manor looked up off his map like a man being handed a rope at the exact moment he had decided to stop drowning.

“You have to be strategic,” he said. “Hit them fast and hard. The dwarf way.”

“That's not strategic,” said Hjumpik.

“That is very much the dwarf way,” said Waluigi, from the chair.

The prince's hand came down on the map and stopped moving. Then he began, and for the first time in three sessions he sounded like somebody who had been taught this by a person.

“Strategic,” he said, “is that you use your brain. Top to bottom. Not all at the same time.” His finger walked the ink. “The monster is going for the middle. Everything it does, it does at the middle — that is where the house is thickest, that is where the food is. So we do not go to the middle. We go around.”

He drew it in the air with two fingers, a wide pair of arms closing.

“Pincer,” Hjumpik said.

“From the back,” the prince agreed. “Maybe.”

“We can try,” said the dwarf, and the whole room leaned in, because *we can try* out of Hjumpik is a promise with a signature on it.

The heir straightened. He had been not-drinking for days and it showed in the way he held his own sleeves, and he said the next part quickly, as if it might be taken back from him.

“Alright. I'll allow you to command a unit. Get five, six people. Lead a charge from whatever point you need. We will figure out the rest with the others from there.”

Six people. In a manor of several hundred, mostly fairies, most of them dancing. Six.

Toad Lee straightened off his axe. Waluigi sat up in the stolen chair.
sections.waluigi_note: Six people. In a manor of several hundred, mostly fairies, most of them dancing, the heir could find six to give away — and gave them to the only person in the room who had never once asked for anything. He had slept less than any of them and still produced the only coherent sentence of the week.

sections.name: Guard the Window
sections.subtitle: the guard who ran, the shaking floor, and a route refused
sections.overview:
The kitchen-sill guard was still in the room, apron over breastplate, towel over elbow, trying very hard to look like furniture.

Hjumpik looked at him the way a man looks at a tool he has already decided to use.

“Guard the window,” he said.

It was the same guard who had gone out of a top-floor window ahead of a hundred-foot flower and landed in a hedge with his dignity mostly intact. The whole house knew. The hedge knew.

“If you're strong,” Hjumpik added, kindly, which was worse, “we can use all the hands we can.”

“Hm,” said the guard. “I guess.”

Then the floor moved.

Not a shudder — a *movement*, the whole room lifting an inch and setting itself down again, and the pins on the map skittered half a hand's width toward the window. Dust came off the rafters in a thin grey curtain. Somewhere far off, wood screamed the way wood screams: one long crack, then a sound like a table being folded.

“What was that,” said Toad Lee. “It's getting closer.”

“I'm not sure. It started shaking.”

“That is not an answer, that is the same thing said twice.”

The Oracle arrived in the doorway without arriving — one moment the frame was empty, the next it was not, and nobody in the room could afterwards say which direction it had come from. It said that the Revel one was having trouble. It said it the way weather reports say *rain*. Then it turned to go and clearly expected to be followed.

Hjumpik did not follow.

“No,” he said. “No, no, no. We go from the outside wall.”

*WAH. Somebody has to say it: the Oracle offered this party a direct route to the Revel and the dwarf said NO, WE'LL TAKE THE LONG WAY, and then walked off. Waluigi has filed that decision under BOTH COLUMNS. Correct, probably. Also the single most expensive sentence spoken in this manor.*
sections.waluigi_note: Hjumpik refused a guided path from the one entity in three planes that has never once lied to him directly. He did it because a guided path puts the guide in charge of the destination. That is a real principle. It is also, on this map, a six-hour detour through a house full of things that eat corridors.

sections.name: The Door Full of Thirst
sections.subtitle: a mob, a slur, and a prophecy
sections.overview:
Outside the war room the corridor was loud, and the loud had a shape: forty-odd fairies and housefolk pressed against a door they could not open, arguing with it. Hands flat on the wood. Breath on the panel. Somebody's knuckles going again, and again, and again.

— *open it. Open the door.* — *there's drink behind that.* — *there's a tree behind that.* — *there's DRINK behind that.*

Hjumpik went into the middle of it the way a wedge goes into a log, and the log opened.

“There is no drink,” he said. “The barrels are splinters. The splinters are under a tree. Go help somebody.”

A satyr with a wine-stained tunic got close enough to smell. “You,” he said. “You can't command anything. You're too broody.”

“Broody.”

“You stand in corners. You look at walls. It's off-putting.”

Hjumpik considered this with total seriousness, the way he considers everything, which is the reason people keep telling him things.

“I might be in charge of them soon,” he said.

The satyr laughed. The corridor laughed with him, in that rolling way crowds do, and then the corridor lost interest, which is the only thing crowds are better at than laughing. They went back to the door. Somebody started singing. It was, unavoidably, the Revel's song, and three of them knew the words.

Hjumpik turned away from the mob and found the two house guards stationed at the foot of the stair, and asked them the question that would define the next four hours.

“Where's my battalion?”

The guards looked at each other. Then they stepped aside — not out of the way, exactly, but out of the *middle* — and one of them said, with the exhausted courtesy of a man delivering bad news he did not write:

“It's dangerous down there, sir.”

*Waluigi has now watched a dwarf ask for an army twice in one week. The first time he was given a map. The second time he was given a hallway and a warning. The manor does not have armies. The manor has whatever is standing near the door when somebody asks.*

sections.name: With My Brawn and Your Brains
sections.subtitle: the recruitment of Toad Lee, and the body already in the hall
sections.overview:
Waluigi stood up out of the stolen chair and said, in the tone of a man proposing a joint venture, that he wanted to be careful.

“Careful,” said Hjumpik.

“Careful.”

“With my brawn,” said the dwarf, “and your brains, we will make it through.”

It was, Waluigi will admit, one of the more accurate sentences anyone has ever said to him, and it landed badly precisely because of that. He accepted it with a sniff and a straightening of his collar.

They went down the stair into air that got colder every step, dust drifting in the thin grey light from a window nobody had bothered to glaze. Halfway along the lower corridor Waluigi stopped, turned around, and shouted back up into the gloom.

“TOAD LEE.”

The Toad came around a corner at a dead run, axe over one shoulder, cap askew, arriving with two full strides to spare — because, as the record must state plainly, nobody had asked him, and he had simply attached himself to the party on the assumption that somebody eventually would. He was almost left in a corridor with a mushroom in it.

“I heard my name,” he said, breathing hard.

“You heard half of it,” said Waluigi.

“That's the important half.”

They reached the muster point: a service hall with a cracked tile floor, a rack of unused serving cloths, and the smell of a house that had stopped cooking. Six people stood in it, in no formation, holding what they had.

“So,” said Waluigi, surveying his new command with the eye of a man appraising a very disappointing estate, “my new battalion.”

“Don't kill them,” said Hjumpik.

“That is a low bar and Waluigi is offended by how low it is.”

Then the door at the end of the service hall opened and a house guard came out carrying a body the way staff carry anything heavy: with both arms, chin tucked, no ceremony available.

Green skin. Green livery under it. A goblin, small, still dressed for service, one shoe missing.

“Who died,” Hjumpik said.

“One of the green goblins,” said the guard, and set him down against the wall with a care that was almost an apology.

“It *was* a green goblin.”

“Sir.”

Waluigi looked at the dead goblin's cuffs. They were folded. Somebody had folded them.

“Why,” he said, “are butlers fighting.”

Nobody answered, because the answer was in the room with them: because there was nobody else. The house had spent its guards on the foyer, its fairies on the Revel, and its tree cutters on the lane, and what was left was a waiter, two goblins off the silver, and a pair of guards who had drawn the short corridor.

“It's not a perfect team,” Hjumpik said, “but this is what we have.”

“They're scraping the barrel,” said Waluigi.

“There *is* no barrel. The tree got the barrels.”

“Then they are scraping the floor, and Waluigi's metaphor survives on a technicality.”

“What's the problem,” Hjumpik said.

“The problem,” said Waluigi, with great pleasure, “is that there is a plant monster, and two dead.”

The dwarf looked down at the small green body with the folded cuffs.

“Sorry. Some of them died. We're trying to make zero casualties with me in command.” And then, quietly, to nobody, “Ho ho ho.”

*Waluigi has attended the funerals of kings, hedge funds, and one extremely expensive hat. This is the first he has attended where the deceased was still holding a serving cloth. Fold the cuffs. That is what you do when there is nothing else to do.*
sections.waluigi_note: Recruitment method, for the record: one Toad, summoned by shouting his name up a stairwell. No muster, no roll, no oath — a dwarf, a liar, a Toad with an axe, and six people who happened to be indoors. Two were dead before the roll call. The archive has one name for them, a green goblin of the household staff, and no name at all for the second.

sections.name: Technically
sections.subtitle: the command dispute, and a plea remembered at the worst possible moment
sections.overview:
“What,” said Waluigi, “I thought *I* was in command.”

“We're both in command,” said Hjumpik. “Technically I'm in command. You're my advisor.”

“What advisor. This is worse than WarioWare.”

“Don't worry. You have more power than WarioWare.” The dwarf's beard twitched, which is where his grin lives. “I guess you'll direct me if anything goes wrong. You take command.”

It was a good offer. It was also, and this is the part the archive must preserve exactly, an offer made in the same breath as the sentence that ended it. Because Waluigi heard *you take command* and answered with the only thing he has ever actually wanted from this dwarf, which is to be listened to.

“Like how you listened,” he said, “during the planar fracture ritual that caused this? To my pleas?”

The corridor went very still. The six recruits looked at their boots. Somewhere above them the floor moved again, an inch, and set itself down.

Hjumpik did not flinch. He also did not look away, which is worse, because it meant he had already thought about it.

“Hm. You could write that in your wahbook or something.” A pause. “But it's not just that. Okay. No need to argue — we got plant monsters coming out.”

And Waluigi, who has been called many things by many governments and none of them *advisor*, wrote it down.

He has the leaf with him now: [[prop:prop_wahbook_command_dispute|one page, in his own hand, headed TECHNICAL]], with the plea transcribed in full beneath it and the word *technically* underlined twice.

“Hm,” he said. “Partial. Fine.”

*WAH! There it is. I said it. I asked him if he had listened during the ritual that caused this. He told me to write it in the wahbook. I wrote it in the wahbook. I always write it in the wahbook. Two men, one hammer, one staff, and a disagreement about who is driving that has now outlived three monsters, one fire, and a calendar.*

sections.name: Randall, Brad, Timmy, Hank, Wyatt
sections.subtitle: a roll call in which every name is a disappointment to somebody
sections.overview:
“Names,” said a goblin.

“Sure,” said Hjumpik.

They went around the circle, six pairs of boots on cracked tile in a hall cold enough to see your breath in. The guard was Randall. The guard after him said his name, once, into the cold. The waiter was Brad, hands still red from a sink he had not stood at in three days. The top guard — the one standing tallest, on purpose, so that somebody would notice he was standing tallest — was Timmy. The goblin with a folded handkerchief in his breast pocket was Hank; the linen was white and square and the only clean thing in the room. The goblin with the white hair was Wyatt.

“You have common names,” Hjumpik said.

“Well,” said the goblin, “fine. It's Randall.”

“That is the same name.”

“It's Randall *now*.”

Waluigi made the list. He has always made the list. It took eleven seconds and it is the only document produced by this battalion that will outlive it.

“Who put you in charge,” one of them asked.

“The map master,” said Hjumpik.

“*Whose* map master.”

“O.C.'s map master.”

That settled it, in the way that two initials settle everything in this family. The recruits did not ask again. The authority had come down off the table in the war room — the heir's map, the heir's pins, the heir's officer — and arrived in a service hall as a dwarf who had been told he could have six.

“You're under my control,” Hjumpik told them, “fortunately or unfortunately.”

Then he gave the speech. It was not long. He is not a long man.

“You're having issues. Some of you guys died. That's a shame. But right now we gotta pick ourselves back up.”

Toad Lee opened a door looking for somewhere to put the dead. It was the mushroom room — the poison one, the coat room that had already eaten a spy — and the mushrooms turned toward the light of the open door like an audience.

“Leave the bodies in the hallway,” Hjumpik said.

They leaned them against the door. He looked at it.

“Against the *wall*.”

They moved them against the wall.

*WAH! I wrote the list. Randall, Brad, Timmy, Hank, Wyatt. The one after Randall said his name. I heard it. I am not printing a first hearing from this house until he says it twice — I have been burned by first-hearings here. That is not the record failing. That is me being careful.*
sections.waluigi_note: “The map master. O.C.'s map master.” Authority in this manor does not come from a person. It comes from a table with pins on it, and whoever is standing at the table when the asking happens. That is worth remembering: it is how the graft in this family has always worked.

sections.name: First Order — The Leaves
sections.subtitle: up top of the wall, and the longsword that found the wrong goblin
sections.overview:
“My first order,” Hjumpik said, “is to try to go up top of the wall. The Revel is the other side. Remove the leaves.”

It was, in its way, the most sensible thing said in the manor in a week. The Revel ate; the leaves were the mouth; the leaves were on the outside of the wall, in the cold grey air, where a man could reach them with his hands without being eaten first.

“I'll let Brad and Hank take care of it,” said the dwarf, “and we can sit back and relax.”

“No,” said Waluigi. “No, no. You should go there too.”

“And what — you stay and watch?”

“Waluigi stays and *directs*. It is a different verb and it is a better one.”

Hjumpik looked at him for a long moment, then at the six, and made the decision the record will judge him kindly for.

“Two guards, two goblins. Timmy leads the charge.”

Timmy straightened so hard his pauldron rang. And Hjumpik went with them — not behind them, not at the back, but shoulder-to-shoulder with a goblin holding a handkerchief and a waiter holding a carving knife — because he had said *pick ourselves back up* out loud, and dwarves are unable to say a thing out loud and then not do it.

Waluigi remained in the service hall.

“I'm checking something,” he announced. “Make sure nothing crazy goes down.”

“Of course,” said Waluigi, to Waluigi. “I only make stylish decisions. Not crazy ones.”

“No friendly fire, please,” Hjumpik called back, and sighed the sigh of a man who already knew.

Then, at the top of the stair, backlit by the grey morning and holding a warhammer that had once been a bell:

“Let's glorify the morning.”

*WAH. Waluigi wishes to state, before the record states it for him, that at some point in the hour that follows he was in a bathroom. It had running water. It had a door that locked. In a house where the corridors eat people, that is not cowardice, that is *logistics*, and he will not be taking questions.*


“TEAM,” Hjumpik roared, “AND AN ENEMY!”

He was pointing at a shrub. The shrub was moving. It came along the wall walk on a hundred small root-feet with the unhurried patience of a thing that has all morning, and every leaf on it turned, one after another, the way a crowd turns to watch a fight.

“You know what to do!”

“ENGAGE,” said Hank, and went.

He was picked up — actually lifted, feet leaving the stone — by Randall, who set him down three paces closer to the shrub, and Hank ran the rest of the way himself with a kitchen knife in each hand and his handkerchief still folded in his pocket. The first knife went in under a leaf-cluster. The shrub made a sound like a wet bedframe.

Its rake came around flat and caught the house guard across the breastplate. Timmy roared and went in with the longsword, twice, in the good old multiattack way —

— and both strokes landed on Hank.

The goblin went down under his own commander's sergeant like a sack dropped off a cart. He got up. He is a goblin; they get up. But something in him had gone thin, and Waluigi, watching from the stair, could see it: the small body shaking itself out and deciding, visibly, that the shrub was now the safer of the two things in the room.

“HEY, GUARD,” Hjumpik shouted. “If you attack the goblin again and actually hit our own men —”

“These guys are puny little things,” said Timmy, defensively, “they won't work unless you put oomf into them!”

“You put oomf into *Hank*.”

“He was in the way.”

“He is on our side.”

“He's very small.”

Hjumpik rubbed his face with a hand the size of a ham.

“You guys need some more just — brain cells.” A beat. “That doesn't make much sense.”

“No,” said Waluigi, “it really doesn't.”

*Waluigi's doctrine has always been that the enemy is whoever is standing where you swing. He has said this at four different governments. Watching it happen to a goblin named Hank, from a staircase, at nine in the morning, has done more for his argument than any of his forty volumes.*
sections.waluigi_note: Two rounds, five turns, four attacks, no spells, one shrub. The only casualty of note was inflicted by the battalion on itself. Hjumpik's order was *no friendly fire please*; the order was given, heard, and immediately spent.

sections.name: Your Job Isn't Over
sections.subtitle: the goblin who did nothing, and a leader who follows
sections.overview:
When the shrub stopped moving — and it did stop, eventually, under enough knives that it ran out of places to be cut — Hjumpik turned around and found the sixth member of his battalion standing exactly where he had been standing at the start.

“What do you do,” Hjumpik said.

The goblin shrugged. It was a magnificent shrug. It had shoulders in it.

“You should have joined,” said the dwarf. “Cut some leaves. Do the small fry. Just keep moving — time's a-wasting.” He jerked his chin down the wall walk. “I think I saw another one around that door, running around.”

“We will handle it,” said Waluigi, magnanimously, from a safe distance.

“No, no, no,” said Hjumpik. “I'm your battalion leader. I'll follow you.”

And he did. Which is the part of this filing Waluigi keeps coming back to, because it is so small and so completely against the man's interest: a dwarf who had been handed six people and could, at any point, have gone back to the war room and pointed at a map like a gentleman. He stayed on a cold wall walk with a waiter and two goblins, cutting leaves off the mouth of the thing that was eating the house, because he had said he would.

They cut for the better part of an hour. Leaves came down in wet armfuls and the cold air smelled of green cut open. Under them the wall was not wall: it was a lattice of green fibre, pale as tendon, running in every direction, and where they cut it, it grew back thicker within the minute.

“Good work,” Hjumpik said, at last. “You're better than I thought.”

The goblins looked at each other. Praise from the dwarf had the effect of sunlight on stone.

“Your job isn't over.”

*WAH. Cutting the leaves off a Revel is like shaving a man who is on fire. The archive has known this since the [poison-plants filing](the_feyward_revel_crisis_poison_plants_and_frozen_diplomacy), which said it in writing, and which nobody read, because the Feyward's only export is advice that arrives one session late.*

sections.name: Above Our Paygrade
sections.subtitle: two doors, one kitchen, and the wood coming through the wall
sections.overview:
At the end of the wall walk there were two doors, and Hjumpik opened the first one, looked into it, and closed it.

He said nothing about what was in it. The record has nothing. Waluigi has asked. The dwarf's exact words, on three separate occasions, have been *no*.

He opened the second. Kitchen. Cold range, a butcher's block with a cleaver still standing in it, sacks of something that had stopped being flour. He ordered it barricaded, and the goblins went at it with the enthusiasm of people given a job that could not kill them.

“What's in there,” Hjumpik said, nodding at the first door.

“Nothing,” said the guard.

The dwarf put a hand on the man's pauldron. It covered the whole thing.

“You're a royal guard, right. You can do it.”

“Yeah,” said the guard. “You're right.” And then, with the sudden flat certainty of a man whose body has already decided: “And my instincts say we should use the other door.”

Hjumpik took a look for himself.

He closed the door. He turned around. And Hjumpik Deldkur — Asset Orange, the Anvil of Disaster Inc., the man who has been lifted, dropped, stabbed with a pen, and nearly eaten by a wall — ran.

“It's above our paygrade,” he said, over his shoulder, at speed.

He regrouped with Waluigi. Waluigi was not there. The door was closed. Behind it, running water.

Some minutes later Waluigi emerged, damp at the cuffs, radiant, entirely composed.

“Ready for adventure,” he said.

“There's a monster,” said Hjumpik.

“How big.”

“Big enough that I ran.”

Waluigi considered this for a full second, which for Waluigi is a long silence, and did not go and look.

*There are two doors in this filing and the archive has one door's worth of information. That is not a gap in the record. That is a dwarf who opened something, closed it, and has since declined three separate requests. Waluigi has stopped asking. He has started writing it down instead.*


They were still arguing about it when the corridor started to fill.

Housefolk came past at a run — satyrs, fairies, a goblin with an armful of candlesticks — all of them saying the same two words in different orders. *Woodfellow. Giant. Support.* The librarian was out on the lane fighting something, and the something was winning enough that people had come inside to fetch help.

“Red alert,” said Timmy. “Red alert.” He stopped dead. “Look in front of you.”

It came down the corridor the way a river comes down a corridor. Not walking — *arriving*, trunk first, with the ceiling coming apart above it in long strips of plaster, and every doorframe it passed exploding outward into splinters. Sap ran down it in ropes.

“Was that the one fighting Woodfellow,” said Brad.

“No,” said Hjumpik. “Even bigger.”

“That was bigger than the one fighting Woodfellow?”

“That *is* bigger.”

“Alright,” said Hjumpik, turning. “Second in command. Time for you to shine.”

Waluigi had three things in him and he named all three, because he is a professional and professionals itemise. One: a wall — force, stone, the whole corridor sealed, and it would cost him most of what he had. Two: hit it directly, ice, straight down the throat of the thing. Three: freeze the room, everything in it, everyone in it.

“No fire,” said Hjumpik.

“Waluigi was not going to use fire. Waluigi has *learned*.”

He chose two.

The ice went in hard and white and absolutely enormous — a lance of it the length of the hallway, cold enough that the plaster cracked on both walls — and the tree drank it. Waluigi watched his own spell go into the bark and disappear the way a cup of water disappears into a horse. Steam came off the thing. Frost formed on it and then was simply *gone*, absorbed, eaten.

“We gotta go,” said Hjumpik.

*WAH. It is a plant. Plants drink. Waluigi, author of FORTY VOLUMES, chose to attack a thirsty tree with a large quantity of water. He would like the record to note that he named three options out loud, in order, with costs attached, and that the room let him pick the second one.*
sections.waluigi_note: Hjumpik ran. The archive files *above our paygrade* as the most useful sentence he has produced in the Feyward: the first time anyone in this house measured a threat honestly instead of heroically. Nobody in the manor had said one all week.

sections.name: Toad Lee and Wyatt Hold the Line
sections.subtitle: the breach, Hank's door, and the mound that got overwhelmed
sections.overview:
It breached.

That is the only word for it. The corridor did not open; it *ceased*, the far wall folding outward into the room beyond in one slow motion, and the tree came through the gap with the debris still hanging off it like a coat.

At the other door, meanwhile, forty thirsty fairies were still arguing with a locked panel about beer.

“Quickly, in here!” Hank was standing in a doorway, waving both arms, his handkerchief finally out of his pocket and being used, for the first time in the record, to wipe his face. The door was small. Behind Hank, through the frame, was the enormous slow shape of the tree monster, arriving at the same door from the other side.

“Bad idea,” Hjumpik said.

Hank went in anyway, handkerchief still in his fist, and the dark swallowed him up to the shoulders.

“We gotta go,” said the dwarf, and turned his back on a goblin, which the archive will note cost him something.

What was left in the corridor was a shambling mound — the second thing, the one that had come through behind the tree, rot and grudge in a shape that had once been a hedge — and what was left to stop it was Toad Lee, Wyatt, and the entire remaining confidence of the sixth detachment.

They held.

The air in there was wet and green and tasted of cold sap. Wyatt went at it twice with the white hair streaming and both hands on the haft, and the mound answered with something that was not a blow — a *spell*, a sour green light that found Brad and put him on his knees in the debris, coughing dust. Toad Lee got his axe into the mass and worked. Hjumpik came back into it and cut.

“Overwhelm it,” he said. “Just — overwhelm it.”

So they did. Six of them, then eight, then whoever came past, all of them hitting the same square yard of rotten hedge until it stopped being a thing and started being a pile. It went down. It stayed down.

“Our team fought valiantly,” said Brad, from the floor, “and defeated it.”

“We just had to overwhelm him,” said Wyatt, “and we were able to get him down.”

Hjumpik tried to cut it further, out of something that was not quite suspicion and not quite respect, and found only wet fibre.

*WAH! Two dead at the roll call, one waiter on the floor, one goblin through a door he was told not to go through, and a hedge killed by committee. The archive would like to point out that the winning move was not a plan. The winning move was six people in the same square yard. Hjumpik's entire battalion is one tactic: be there.*
sections.waluigi_note: Hank went through the door alone. He is alive in the later record, which means either the room was survivable or goblins are. The archive has no door report. It has, however, a dwarf who turned his back and has not mentioned it since.

sections.name: A Glass of Wine, a Roast Chestnut
sections.subtitle: the reading, the speech, and the monster that arrived during both
sections.overview:
In the room beyond, while the corridor was still being decided, Waluigi had found a chair, a shelf, and an audience.

The book was water-warped and somebody else's — essays, in a hand from before the fracture, about how little a person needs. He read aloud to the survivors in a voice that had carried across three courtrooms:

> *I felt once more how simple and frugal a thing is happiness: a glass of wine, a roast chestnut, a wretched little brazier, the sound of the sea.*

The fairies listened. One of them was crying. It may have been about the chestnuts.

“That's what we must do,” Waluigi announced, closing the book with a slap. “Fight for a better future! Wahahaha! I am leader, and my future is the best.”

“Hey, Waluigi,” said Hjumpik, from the doorway. “Uhh. You know what's happening right now?”

“Waluigi is inspiring people.”

“There is a monster about to eat you.”

The far wall came in. Not the tree this time — the other one, the biggest of them, the thing the whole house had been feeling through its floorboards since breakfast, arriving with a sound like a cathedral clearing its throat. Plaster went up in a white sheet. Somebody's chair went under.

“Well,” said Waluigi, standing up with the book still in his hand, “I just held an inspirational speech, right. So that means something, right.”

It did not mean something. What meant something was the next eleven minutes, which the record reconstructs from the tally and from who was still standing: the Oracle going at a shrub twice and going at it hard; House Guard Joseph and a second house guard on the mound; a satyr berserker and a satyr scout and a satyr whose name nobody got, all three of them into the treant; two sprites working the same treant with spells from opposite ends of the room; a goblin with a staff; and, busiest of everything on that floor and classified by nobody since, the thing the tally calls the Ravenous Host.

The sprite archer did nothing. The sprite archer did nothing for the entire engagement and survived it, which is the only genuinely clever thing anyone did.

They won. The floor went quiet. Dust came down off what was left of the ceiling for a long time afterwards, like snow with an attitude.

*Waluigi's speech was eleven words long and the monster arrived at word nine. He would like it noted that the room was still listening when it came through the wall, and that no amount of botany changes that.*

sections.name: Order of the Revel
sections.subtitle: an evacuation signed by the thing being evacuated from
sections.overview:
The order came up the stair ahead of the people carrying it: a house guard with a rolled sheet in one fist, shouting it at everybody he passed.

“You civilians! We're evacuating! Order of the Revel!”

Waluigi has the paper. It is [[prop:prop_revel_evacuation_order|short, warm, and signed in the Revel's own office]], which is a sentence he never expected to be able to write. A house being eaten was being cleared for its own safety by the eater's staff, on the eater's authority, with the eater's seal on it, and the fairies obeyed it without a single question, because in this house the music is the government.

“I need to help some guys up there,” Hjumpik said.

“You sure you want to fight that,” said the guard, “and not evacuate to the upper flowers?”

Toad Lee arrived then, cap straight, chest out, five Toads in a wedge behind him.

“I gathered a squad,” he said. “A Toad squad. I'm pretty proud of them.”

He was. It showed. They were also, Waluigi noted, the only unit in the manor that had arrived already in formation.

Hjumpik pointed the evacuators at the one man doing the evacuating and told them to help him, and then — on orders from the Revel, delivered by a guard, in a house the Revel was consuming — decided to go the other way.

A satyr fell in beside them on the stair, hooves on stone, wine still on his breath.

“I want to join the tree protectors,” he said. “If you can't beat them, join them.”

“They want to kill you,” said Hjumpik.

“I'll show you they don't want to attack us.”

Hjumpik put him in an arm hold. It was not violent. It was total. The satyr's feet left the step and stayed off it.

“Why don't you evacuate the civilians,” the dwarf said, “and not be an idiot.”

“Alright, alright — you're clearly stronger than me.”

“They don't call me Hjumpik for nothing.”

*Nobody has ever explained to Waluigi what they call him for. He has asked. He has asked in three planes. The name is a verb in a language with one speaker, and the speaker uses it on people.*
sections.waluigi_note: The Revel issued an evacuation order to protect the house from itself, and the house complied. That is not incompetence. That is what total authority looks like from the inside: the fire brigade reports to the fire, and everyone still lines up.

sections.name: Stretched Thin
sections.subtitle: a commander who is in control, a room that is not, and reinforcements refused
sections.overview:
They moved through two more rooms. The second one had a commander in it, standing very upright in front of a door that was bulging.

“The situation is under control,” he said.

Behind him the door bowed outward an inch, held, and bowed again.

“It doesn't look good,” said Hjumpik. Then, quieter, mostly to himself: “Maybe we should release the Revel.”

He thought about it for four full steps. The book in Woodfellow's library had said what a starving Revel does — it turns on the room. Release it and the music stops, and then the thing that was dancing starts eating, and there is no version of that which ends with a house in it.

*Maybe not,* he decided, and kept walking.

From the room they had just left came the sound of a great deal of slashing — steel on something wet, over and over, and underneath it a thin high note that might have been a fairy and might have been a hinge.

Hjumpik stopped. He looked back through the doorframe, one hand on the frame, dust coming off his beard. He looked at the two guards beside him.

“There is a lot of slashing,” he said. “You guys going to do something?”

“And leave the Oracle — the *heir*, I mean — like, just alone?” The guard's voice had the specific hurt of a man correcting himself in public. “No. Our job is to guard him.”

“No. I mean reinforcements.”

“Well,” said the guard, “we're pretty stretched thin as is.”

The slashing went on. The record has the shape of it from the tally: sprites coming and going, a sprite caster taking a multiattack through the ribs and going down, a sprite archer retreating four separate times, a sprite warrior's blade finding the sprite archer instead of the enemy, a sorcerer attacking three times and running three times, and Woodfellow, the treant, the dryad and the satyr druid Zach all recorded as doing nothing at all — which in the middle of that corridor meant *holding still and being the thing everything else was fighting around*.

Everybody fell back. Everybody. Including, eventually, the door.

*WAH. "Our job is to guard him." In a house on fire, with a monster three rooms away, the garrison's answer to a request for help was a job description. Waluigi has worked for institutions. He recognises the tone. It is the tone of people who have been told so many times what they are for that they can no longer hear what is being asked.*

sections.name: The Bait
sections.subtitle: an armhold's worth of arithmetic, and the name of a dead dwarf
sections.overview:
Back in the war room: Waluigi in the chair, Hjumpik on his feet, guards around the table, the map under everybody's elbows with three new pins in it that nobody remembered adding.

“What can we do,” somebody said. “Is there a way to stop this?”

“There's always a way,” said Hjumpik, “but it might be difficult. There are multiple of them.” He put a fist on the table. “I say we sneak attack. We let them come in, and as the bait runs, we gang up on them.”

“Alright, I guess we could do that.”

“Hjumpik is not being bait.”

“Well, *Waluigi* is not being the bait,” said Waluigi. “How about Toad Lee. He's nimble, right. We slap a piece of meat on him from the kitchen, he runs into the room, and we all trap it.”

“I was thinking maybe a fairy could be the bait,” said Hjumpik. “Like a fly.”

A fairy came in. A guard grabbed him — one hand, closed almost all the way. The room looked at the small winged thing in the guard's fist, at the dust coming off him in the cold light, and something in it turned over.

“No,” said Hjumpik. “No, no. We should not pick a random fairy.”

“Why?”

“It's not good to do.”

“Say if I toss you in there,” said the guard, “you'd want to —” and then he explained himself, and the explanation was worse than the offer. If a good fairy dies, he said, we are already wearing thin. If a *mediocre* fairy dies, a good one can take its place.

“Very doomer way to think,” said Hjumpik.

“It's arithmetic.”

“It's arithmetic about people.” The dwarf folded his arms. “I say we get a warrior fairy. The bait won't die — we will just attract him. We need a nimble person, less likely to get caught.”

A goblin left the room without asking. He came back with a fairy under one arm: battered, bruised, one wing bent at an angle wings do not bend, eyes open and entirely clear.

“I can take him,” the goblin said.

Hjumpik looked at the fairy for a long time.

“You remind me of my grandpa.”

“What was he like?”

“Dead.” A beat. “But a great warrior.”

“So I'm going to die.”

“Even when his arm was cut off,” Hjumpik said, “he still wanted to fight. I saw his drive. It's in you.”

“What was his name?”

“Piktor Deldkur the Third.”

Waluigi wrote it down before the sentence was finished.

“Toad Lee is still more practical,” he said. “We know him. He is less likely to die.”

“He is a Toad,” said Hjumpik. “But he will not do it.”

And then the plan, whole, in one breath, from a dwarf who had been given six people that morning and had four left:

“We shoot him first. Get his attention. As he runs after you, my guys will be in position. As he runs by, you run out of there. We surprise attack him. Gang up on him. Kill him.” He shrugged. “Can't go wrong.”

*WAH. Piktor Deldkur the THIRD. Third. There is a First and a Second in a grave somewhere, and Hjumpik has just told a room full of strangers that his family's inheritance is an arm and an attitude. Waluigi has forty volumes and none of them contain a Deldkur. That ends tonight.*
sections.waluigi_note: The bait plan has one load-bearing assumption and it is the sentence *can't go wrong*: that the thing chasing the bait will keep chasing. Every monster in this manor so far has stopped, turned, or gone somewhere else. Hjumpik's plan is the first one built on the enemy behaving.

aftermath:
**Standing.** The Overgrown Manor is one corridor smaller and one evacuation order larger. The leaves on the outside wall were cut and have grown back thicker. The largest of the plant monsters is down in the room where Waluigi was reading; the corridor it came through is not held, it is merely quiet. The Revel has not ended. It has, however, demonstrated that it can order its own house evacuated and be obeyed without argument, which is the most frightening sentence in this filing and Waluigi would like it read twice.

**Personnel.** Hjumpik commands a detachment of six, of whom four are standing, one is on the floor talking, and one is somewhere behind a door he went through alone. Toad Lee has a Toad squad of five and is, by a wide margin, the only officer in the manor whose unit arrived in formation. The house guard refused reinforcements twice in one night, both times citing the heir. The Oracle offered a direct route to the Revel and was told no; it fought anyway, twice, at a shrub.

**Materiel.** Retained: the [OC soul ring](oc_soul_ring), [Morel's key](morel_feyward_key), and [Steely's rusted fragments](steely_rusted_fragments), all still in Hjumpik's pocket, all still unburied. Expended: one ice lance the length of a hallway, absorbed entire; a quantity of leaves; one kitchen; one corridor wall; two housefolk. Acquired: [[prop:prop_feyward_sixth_detachment_commission|a commission nobody signed]], [[prop:prop_revel_evacuation_order|an evacuation order from the Revel office]], and a name — Piktor Deldkur the Third.

**Exposure.** The house now knows the party commands people, which is different from knowing the party fights. Hjumpik's authority rests on a table with pins on it and an office nobody has ever met. And one combatant in the largest engagement of the night is on the tally under a name the archive has never seen before or since: the Ravenous Host.
waluigiAssessment:
**1. The battalion is a tactic, and the tactic is being there.** Four engagements, no formation, no flank, no plan that survived contact with a shrub. The mound died because six people hit the same square yard until it stopped being a thing. That is not generalship. It is the only generalship this house has, and it worked three times out of four, and the archive is professionally obliged to say so while noting that it does not scale.

**2. Friendly fire is the Feyward's actual weapon.** Timmy put two strokes into Hank. A sprite warrior put a blade into a sprite archer. On the lane, a satyr scout's shaft took Swifty and Bramm's first cut found Renard. Three separate engagements, same signature. The wood does not need to outfight this house. It needs the house to keep swinging in the dark, which it will, because there is no light and everybody is frightened.

**3. Ice was the wrong answer and Waluigi knew it in time to not care.** A plant drinks. He named three options with costs attached — the wall, the strike, the whole room frozen — and picked the one that looked best from a staircase. The room let him. That is the finding: not that the archivist erred, but that nobody in the manor is willing to overrule anybody else, which is what a house looks like when its government is a song.

**4. The Revel is a schedule, not a siege.** Its own office ordered the upper floors evacuated, promised the music would resume, and was obeyed without a single question. The library volume was right: total surrender, or somebody willing to be the one who stopped the music. Nobody has volunteered. The war room proposed going for the Revelmaster instead and rejected the idea in one line without ever establishing who he is.

**5. Authority in this manor is furniture.** The commission is unsigned. Its authority is *the map master, O.C.'s map master* — a role, attached to a table, attached to two initials that have already turned up carved into bedframes and struck onto soul hardware. A dwarf was put in command of six people by an office nobody has met. The same mechanism, run once more with a different dwarf, is how this family has always worked.

**RECOMMENDATION:** Do not run the bait plan until somebody establishes whether the thing being baited keeps chasing. Every monster in this manor so far has stopped, turned, or gone somewhere else. Hjumpik's plan is the first one built on the enemy behaving, and it rests entirely on *can't go wrong*. Find the Revelmaster. Bury Steely. And ask the dwarf, once, quietly, about the First and Second Piktor Deldkur.
